mansa-musa.name: Mansa Musa
mansa-musa.summary: Ninth ruler of the Mali Empire (c. 1280–c. 1337), whose reign marked its peak of power and prestige; contemporaries described his wealth from gold and salt trade as almost impossible to measure.

mali-empire.name: Mali Empire
mali-empire.summary: A West African empire from about 1235 to 1610, founded by Sundiata Keita and renowned for the wealth of rulers like Mansa Musa; at its peak the largest empire in West Africa.

bambouk.name: Bambouk
bambouk.summary: Traditional territory in eastern Senegal and western Mali, home to the Bambouk Mountains and historically a source of gold.

ibn-battuta.name: Ibn Battuta
ibn-battuta.summary: A Maghrebi Muslim traveller and scholar (1304–1368/69) from Tangier who journeyed about 117,000 km across Africa, Asia and the Iberian Peninsula and dictated an account of his travels, the Rihla.

gao.name: Gao
gao.summary: A city in Mali on the River Niger, once a major trans-Saharan trade hub; it became capital of the Songhai Empire under Sunni Ali (1464–1492) after earlier being part of the Mali Empire.

sudano-sahelian-architecture.name: Sudano-Sahelian architecture
sudano-sahelian-architecture.summary: An indigenous West African building style using mudbrick and adobe plaster with protruding wooden beams, seen in structures like the Great Mosque of Djenné.

djenn.name: Djenné
djenn.summary: Historic town in central Mali closely tied to Timbuktu through trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold and slaves, famed for its adobe Sudano-Sahelian architecture.

oba-of-benin.name: Oba of Benin
oba-of-benin.summary: Traditional royal title of the ruler of the Kingdom of Benin, held since the Oba dynasty began around the 12th century; the last independent Oba was exiled after the British sacked the capital in 1897.

sankor-madrasah.name: Sankoré Madrasa
sankor-madrasah.summary: A medieval mosque and centre of learning in Timbuktu, founded in the 14th or early 15th century, where individual scholars taught private students rather than a formal university.

tuareg-people.name: Tuareg people
tuareg-people.summary: A traditionally nomadic Amazigh (Berber) ethnic group of the Sahara, numbering 4 to 5 million, who controlled key trans-Saharan trade routes and helped spread Islam in North Africa.

great-mosque-of-djenn.name: Great Mosque of Djenné
great-mosque-of-djenn.summary: The largest adobe brick building in the world, in Djenné, Mali; first built around the 13th century, with the current structure dating from 1907.

oguola.name: Oguola
oguola.summary: Fifth Oba of the Kingdom of Benin, reigning around 1280 to 1295, credited with starting the Benin walls and moats and advancing brass and bronze casting there.

if.name: Ile-Ife
if.summary: An ancient Yoruba city in southwestern Nigeria founded between 1000 and 500 BC, famed by 900 AD for sophisticated bronze, stone and terracotta art.

lost-wax-casting.name: Lost-wax casting
lost-wax-casting.summary: A casting process, also called investment casting or cire perdue, used to duplicate sculptures in metal; the oldest known examples are about 6,500 years old.

inner-niger-delta.name: Inner Niger Delta
inner-niger-delta.summary: An inland river delta of the Niger River, an area of wetlands, lakes and floodplains in the semi-arid Sahel of central Mali, just south of the Sahara.

ghana-empire.name: Ghana Empire
ghana-empire.summary: An ancient West African empire based in what is now southeast Mauritania and western Mali, first mentioned in writing in 830 CE; it became a vassal of the Mali Empire in the 13th century.

al-bakri.name: Al-Bakri
al-bakri.summary: Arab Andalusian historian and geographer (c. 1040-1094) whose writings on the medieval Maghreb are an early source on West African kingdoms.

benin-city.name: Benin City
benin-city.summary: Today the capital of Edo State in southern Nigeria and Nigeria's fourth-largest city, historically the seat of the Oba's palace.

songhai-empire.name: Songhai Empire
songhai-empire.summary: A major West African state that flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries, eventually surpassing the Mali Empire in area, wealth and power under Sonni Ali and later the Askia dynasty.

sonni-ali.name: Sonni Ali
sonni-ali.summary: The 15th ruler of the Sunni dynasty of the Songhai Empire, reigning about 1464 to 1492, who transformed it into an empire by conquering Timbuktu, Massina, the Inner Niger Delta and Djenne.

jolof-empire.name: Jolof Empire
jolof-empire.summary: A Wolof state in what is now Senegal that ruled parts of Mauritania and Gambia from the mid-14th century until 1549.

samori-ture.name: Samori Ture
samori-ture.summary: Malinke Muslim cleric and military strategist (c. 1830–1900) who founded a West African empire and resisted French colonial rule from 1882 until his capture in 1898.

sundiata-keita.name: Sundiata Keita
sundiata-keita.summary: Prince and founder of the Mali Empire (c. 1217 – c. 1255), great-uncle of Mansa Musa; his life is known through oral tradition and the Epic of Sundiata.

keita-dynasty.name: Keita dynasty
keita-dynasty.summary: The ruling Muslim dynasty of pre-imperial and imperial Mali from the 11th to early 17th century, claiming descent from Bilal ibn Rabah; its first mansa was Sundiata Keita.

soumaoro-kant.name: Soumaoro Kanté
soumaoro-kant.summary: 13th-century king of the Sosso people who seized the former capital of the Ghana Empire and conquered neighboring states before being defeated by Sundiata Keita around 1235.

sosso-empire.name: Sosso Empire
sosso-empire.summary: A West African kingdom that broke away from the Ghana Empire and conquered it, peaking under Soumaoro Kanté before being defeated by the rising Mali Empire around 1235.

oualata.name: Oualata
oualata.summary: A small oasis town in southeast Mauritania that served as an important caravan city and southern terminus of a trans-Saharan trade route in the 13th and 14th centuries; now a World Heritage Site.

gajaaga.name: Gajaaga (Galam)
gajaaga.summary: A Soninke kingdom on the upper Senegal River, known as the Land of Gold for its gold exports, that existed from before 1000 CE until 1858 and was a vassal of Jolof and Takrur.

yatenga-province.name: Yatenga
yatenga-province.summary: A former Mossi kingdom in what is now Burkina Faso, whose capital Ouahigouya housed its traditional rulers before its influence declined under French colonization.

mansa-sakura.name: Sakura
mansa-sakura.summary: A usurper, possibly a former slave, who ruled the Mali Empire in the late 13th century, expanded its territory and trade, then was killed returning from the hajj in the early 1300s.

sulayman-of-mali.name: Mansa Sulayman
sulayman-of-mali.summary: Ruler of the Mali Empire in the mid-14th century and brother of Mansa Musa; his death around 1359 triggered a civil war that is seen as ending Mali's golden age.

mari-djata-ii-of-mali.name: Mari Djata II (Jata)
mari-djata-ii-of-mali.summary: Mansa of Mali from 1360 to 1374 and grandson of Mansa Musa; an ineffective, tyrannical ruler whose reign is seen as the start of the empire's decline.

gao-saney.name: Gao-Saney
gao-saney.summary: An archaeological site near Gao in Mali, likely the historical trading town of Sarneh, occupied roughly 700–1100 CE and involved in glass and copper trade networks.

niger-river.name: Niger River
niger-river.summary: The main river of West Africa, running about 4,180 kilometres in a crescent shape through southwest Mali before reaching the Atlantic Ocean; Africa's third-longest river.

ibn-fadlallah-al-umari.name: Ibn Fadlallah al-Umari
ibn-fadlallah-al-umari.summary: An Arab historian from Damascus (1301–1349) whose writings, drawn from accounts of Malian pilgrims, are a primary source describing Mansa Musa's legendary hajj and the gold he gave away in Egypt.

mamluk-sultanate.name: Mamluk Sultanate
mamluk-sultanate.summary: A state ruling Egypt, the Levant and the Hejaz from the mid-13th to early 16th century, governed by a military caste of former slave soldiers, with Cairo as its capital.

sudanian-savanna.name: Sudanian savanna
sudanian-savanna.summary: A broad belt of tropical savanna stretching across Africa between the Sahara and the equatorial forests, historically referred to as "the Sudan" by medieval travelers.

za-dynasty.name: Za dynasty
za-dynasty.summary: Ruling dynasty of the Gao Empire based at Kukiya and Gao on the Niger River, from which the Songhai people and the Sonni dynasty of Sunni Ali descended.

almoravid-dynasty.name: Almoravid dynasty
almoravid-dynasty.summary: Berber Muslim dynasty (1050s-1147) centered in Morocco that built an empire across the western Maghreb and Muslim Spain, founding Marrakesh around 1070.

askia-muhammad-i.name: Askia Muhammad I
askia-muhammad-i.summary: First ruler of Songhai's Askia dynasty (1493-1528), known as Askia the Great, who expanded the empire to its largest extent and built up trade, schools and Islam.

al-maghili.name: Al-Maghili
al-maghili.summary: Berber Sunni scholar (1440-1505) from Tlemcen who advised Askia Muhammad the Great of the Songhai Empire and played a major role in Islamizing West Africa.

muhammad-al-idrisi.name: al-Idrisi
muhammad-al-idrisi.summary: Arab Muslim geographer and cartographer (1100–1165) who served King Roger II in Sicily and created the Tabula Rogeriana, one of the most advanced medieval world maps.

ibn-khaldun.name: Ibn Khaldun
ibn-khaldun.summary: An Arab Tunisian scholar and historian (1332–1406), best known for the Muqaddimah, a foundational work in historiography, sociology and economics.

abu-al-hasan-ali-ibn-uthman.name: Abu al-Hasan Ali
abu-al-hasan-ali-ibn-uthman.summary: Marinid sultan who ruled parts of Morocco from 1331 to 1348, capturing Gibraltar and extending control over Tlemcen and Ifriqiya before losing power and dying in exile in 1351.

nehemia-levtzion.name: Nehemia Levtzion
nehemia-levtzion.summary: Israeli scholar of African and Islamic history (1935–2003) and president of the Open University of Israel from 1987 to 1992.

catalan-atlas.name: Catalan Atlas
catalan-atlas.summary: Medieval world map created around 1375 by Jewish cartographer Cresques Abraham, described as the most important map of the Middle Ages in Catalan.

antonio-malfante.name: Antonio Malfante
antonio-malfante.summary: Genoese trader (died 1450) who traveled to Africa in 1447 for the Centurione Bank and wrote a letter describing trans-Saharan trade and the Niger River near Timbuktu.

koumbi-saleh.name: Koumbi Saleh
koumbi-saleh.summary: A ruined ancient and medieval city site in southeast Mauritania, long thought to be the capital of the Ghana Empire, occupied roughly from the 5th to 14th centuries.

kouroukan-fouga.name: Kouroukan Fouga
kouroukan-fouga.summary: The traditional constitution of the Mali Empire, established after the 1235 Battle of Krina by an assembly of nobles, later recognized by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.

diarra.name: Diarra
diarra.summary: A West African clan name linked to the Kingdom of Diarra, which existed from the 7th century until the 19th century.

musa-ii-of-mali.name: Musa II
musa-ii-of-mali.summary: Mansa of the Mali Empire from 1374 to 1387, who rejected his father's tyranny but was overshadowed by a powerful vizier while eastern provinces around Gao broke away.

takedda.name: Takedda
takedda.summary: A town and former kingdom in present-day Niger, believed to correspond to the archaeological site at Azelik wan Birni.

berbers.name: Berbers
berbers.summary: Indigenous ethnic group of North Africa, known since ancient Egyptian times, who formed kingdoms such as Numidia before Arabization and conversion to Islam from the 7th century.

mandinka-people.name: Mandinka
mandinka-people.summary: A West African ethnic group descended from the Mali Empire, founded in the 13th century under Sundiata Keita; about 15 million strong today, mainly in Mali, Guinea and The Gambia.

tlemcen.name: Tlemcen
tlemcen.summary: The second-largest city in northwestern Algeria, a historic center of the Maghreb blending Arab, Berber, Andalusi, and Ottoman influences.

dendi-people.name: Dendi people
dendi-people.summary: Ethnic group in Benin, Niger, Nigeria and northern Togo along the Niger River, part of the Songhai people and historically the Dendi province of the Songhai Empire.

tarikh-al-sudan.name: Tarikh al-Sudan
tarikh-al-sudan.summary: A West African chronicle written in Arabic around 1655 by a Timbuktu scholar, considered the single most important primary source for the history of the Songhai Empire.

ibadism.name: Ibadism
ibadism.summary: A distinct branch of Islam alongside Sunni and Shia Islam, rooted in the Kharijite movement, that spread from Basra to Oman, North Africa and East Africa.

mand-peoples.name: Mandé peoples
mand-peoples.summary: A broader grouping of West African peoples, including the Mandinka, who speak related Mande languages and share a common caste system, predominantly Muslim today.

tarikh-al-fattash.name: Tarikh al-fattash
tarikh-al-fattash.summary: A West African chronicle covering the Songhai Empire from 1464 to 1599, later shown to combine an authentic 17th-century text with a 19th-century forgery falsely attributed to an earlier author.

mahmud-kati.name: Mahmud Kati
mahmud-kati.summary: An African Muslim Songhai scholar (1468?–1552 or 1593) traditionally credited as author of the West African chronicle Tarikh al-fattash, though this authorship is contested.

soninke-people.name: Soninke
soninke-people.summary: A West African Mande-speaking ethnic group who founded the ancient empire of Ghana (Wagadou), around 200 to 1240 CE, later spreading widely as traders.

angelino-dulcert.name: Angelino Dulcert
angelino-dulcert.summary: Italian-Majorcan cartographer active around 1339, known for two notable portolan charts, including the 1339 chart, the first ever produced in Palma.

jacopo-russo.name: Jacopo Russo
jacopo-russo.summary: A Sicilian Renaissance mapmaker who created illustrated portolan charts, including a 1525 Mansa Musa Map of Mali now held by the British Library.
